content.thinking: I'm drafting the postmortem now, keeping the executive summary focused on what broke, the six-minute duration, and who was affected without inventing figures or overstating confidence. I need to be careful to flag that the Redis config port change as root cause was inferred from deploy timing and logs rather than directly confirmed, and that Redis's own health was never actually checked, while noting the rollback restored baseline and some error-rate elevation may have predated the incident.

assumptions: The cause is inferred from correlation, not proven: the only production change in the preceding two hours landed at 16:03, exactly at onset, and the cache-connection errors start in the same minute. No one inspected the deployed configuration diff to confirm the port value changed.

Redis's own health was never checked. No evidence was gathered to rule out the cache instance being down or unreachable for reasons unrelated to the deploy; that hypothesis was considered and left untested.

The competing hypothesis — that the deploy shipped a code change to the cache client rather than a config change — was never tested and would have been mitigated identically by the rollback. Rollback success therefore does not distinguish between the two.

Recovery is judged from the service returning to its baseline metrics after the rollback, observed about twelve seconds after the action. No independent check (e.g. cache hit ratio back at its prior level over a sustained period) was recorded.

The account-page ClientDisconnected errors appear in the logs from before the onset as well as during it, so some of the error-rate figure attributed to this window reflects pre-existing behaviour rather than the cache failure.
No feature-flag changes were found, so flags are assumed not to be a contributing factor.
The draft pull request is unreviewed and unmerged; it is not yet a fix.
input.executive_summary: On 25 September 2026, customer account pages on the shop were slow for roughly six minutes, from 16:03 to 16:09 UTC, when they recovered. During that window the page-load time for account pages rose sharply and a small additional share of requests failed on top of the errors the service was already returning before the incident began; the exact figures are in the impact section of the incident record. Shoppers browsing other parts of the site were not affected. The cause was a change released to production at the start of the window. Automated response picked up the alert, identified the release as the likely cause, and reverted it; the service was confirmed back to its normal behaviour immediately afterwards. A draft code change to prevent a recurrence has been opened for review. Note that the automated system held the incident for only a small fraction of the outage window — that number describes how quickly the response ran, not how long customers were affected.
input.root_cause: A production deploy to io-shop at 16:03 UTC changed the Redis cache connection configuration to an endpoint that was not accepting connections (port 6380), so every summary-cache lookup on the account-page path failed with "connection refused"; with the cache effectively gone, the render path fell back to uncached work and latency rose far enough to trip the HighLatency alert. Rolling the service back off that revision returned it to baseline, which is the strongest evidence for this cause — the investigator ranked it first at 0.72 confidence, above an alternative that the same deploy shipped a code change to the cache client's connection logic (0.25, never tested) and an independent Redis outage (0.10, never tested; no Redis health data was ever retrieved).
